rv.q: Now, I honestly can’t find fault with it.
This fusillade of laser-focused facetiousness feels like the perfect piffle for our turbulent times.
Ditto Patrick Marber's blissfully silly show — but this one should run and run.
The time is demonstrably right for a comedy whose only real purpose is to put a spring in its audience’s step.
It’s still a winningly funny proposition for a new generation – and Marber pulls out all the stops to raise the Garrick roof.
At its heart, it’s rather sweet: a ridiculous love-letter to friendship and to the sheer craziness and passion of show business.
The jokes are rapid, the satire outrageous.
The sheer ridiculous over-the-top-ness is an ebullient joy that wins over even the hardest (feminist) hearts.
It’s a very pleasurable show, that has a fundamentally funny central premise, and genuinely great songs from Brooks himself.
The Producers has come back to the West End just at the right time, offering a giant slab of feel-good escapism and genuine hilarity when such things feel in short supply.
Patrick Marber's production is a sparkling, comedic masterpiece.
If you want non-stop giggles, gloriously provocative jokes and an easy escape from everyday misery, there’s no better place to be right now than the Garrick.
Resistance is futile when the comedy value is as relentless and impressive as it is in this delightful production.
The Producers is so totally tasteless but so funny.
Just as importantly, it’s a rattling good night out in these troubled times.

As directed by Patrick Marber, the party scene where our devious pair attempt to cajole a pseud-director Roger Debris (Trevor Ashley) and his largely pointless camp side-kick, is particularly lacking in sophistication and resorts too often to slap-stick and lewd kitsch.
His performance is, at times, muted compared with the other talent on stage, but he is a grounding presence in a production that sparkles with eccentricity.
Outrageous, audacious and utterly unmissable, this West End revival is a triumph of impeccable casting, razor-sharp direction and a laugh-a-minute script.
Whatever it is that was missing has certainly been found this time around, as the West End transfer is an obvious five-star show.

The fact that I physically squirmed at certain scenes, especially considering recent events in America, and then questioned my response – all while having an absolute blast – is pure testament to what an inspired show this is.
I genuinely can’t think of anybody who would not enjoy this, except perhaps for the actual real-life Nazis who, terrifyingly enough, remain an extant demographic.
Whether you're nostalgic for The Producers movie or you're looking for a fun-filled night at the theatre, Mel Brooks's The Producers at the Garrick Theatre won't disappoint.
The Producers really is an outstanding collective production where every performer shows up and delivers.
The Producers is the perfect antidote to our troubled times.
From the outset, it's sheer delight.
The Producers sparkled and glowed with Trevor Ashley, perhaps, sparkling more than anyone and loving every glittery second of it.
But perhaps it is enough just to say you don’t miss Mostel for a single moment of this revival’s two and half hours, which could not even be said of Nathan Lane’s performance.
'The Producers' review - Ridiculous, rapid-fire comedy. Mel Brooks’ musical transfers to the West End’s Garrick Theatre after a sell-out run at Menier Chocolate Factory.
The West End’s most shocking show
Brooks and Marber’s wacky giggle-fest in which the crooks are loveable and all the weirdos are endearing is perfectly timed, if bittersweet, escapism.

cn.t: Critics hail this riotous revival as gloriously funny and perfectly timed, with Marber's direction mining every laugh from Brooks' irreverent satire. A few note dated gender politics, but most find it an irresistible comic masterclass.

vr.q: I really enjoyed this production and I loved getting to go and see it at the Garrick.
